title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
description:
# Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown

You are given an integer array `prices`, where `prices[i]` is the price of one stock on day `i`.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve. You may complete as many transactions as you want, but you must obey both rules:

* You may hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before buying again.
* After you sell on day `i`, you cannot buy on day `i + 1`. That next day is a one-day cooldown.

You may also choose to make no transaction.

## Example 1:

**Input:** prices = [1,2,3,0,2]
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** One optimal plan is buy on day 0, sell on day 1, cooldown on day 2, buy on day 3, and sell on day 4.

## Example 2:

**Input:** prices = [1]
**Output:** 0
**Explanation:** A single day cannot complete a buy-sell transaction.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= prices.length <= 5000`
* `0 <= prices[i] <= 1000`

solutions.name: Rolling Three-State DP
solutions.description:
## Approach
Track three end-of-day states: `hold` means holding one share, `sold` means sold today, and `rest` means not holding and not just sold today. On each price, sell from the previous hold state, buy only from the previous rest state, and move a previous sold state into rest.

## Key Insight
The cooldown is enforced by the state graph. A buy transition cannot come from `sold`; it can only come from `rest`, so the day immediately after a sale is forced to pass through rest before another buy can happen.

## Complexity Analysis
Each day updates a constant number of states, so the time complexity is O(n). Only three rolling state values are stored, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Three-Array State Table
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store the same three states in arrays so every day's transition is visible. `hold[day]` is best while holding, `sold[day]` is best after selling that day, and `rest[day]` is best while not holding and not selling that day.

## Key Insight
The table form is a readable trace of the finite-state machine. `hold[day]` may buy only from `rest[day - 1]`, while `rest[day]` may come from either continuing to rest or cooling down from yesterday's sale.

## Complexity Analysis
The algorithm performs one constant-time transition per state per day, so the time complexity is O(n). The three arrays each have length n, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Top-Down Cooldown Memoization
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use `dfs(day, holding)` for the maximum future profit from a day and a holding state. If holding, choose between selling today and jumping to `day + 2`, or continuing to hold. If not holding, choose between buying today and skipping.

## Key Insight
Selling is the only action that creates the cooldown. The recursive transition `sell = prices[day] + dfs(day + 2, 0)` encodes the rule directly and prevents accidental rebuying on the next day.

## Complexity Analysis
There are `2 * n` memoized states and each state compares two choices, so the time complexity is O(n). The memo table and recursion stack use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Hold-Cash Cooldown Lookback
solutions.description:
## Approach
Keep `hold[day]` as the best profit while holding after day `day`, and `cash[day]` as the best profit while not holding after day `day`. Selling can use yesterday's hold. Buying on day `day` can only use `cash[day - 2]`, because `day - 1` would be a cooldown if it was a sell day.

## Key Insight
Instead of naming a separate cooldown state, this route shifts the buy transition back by two days. The index lookback is exactly the rule: after selling, one full day must pass before another buy.

## Complexity Analysis
The loop visits each price once, so the time complexity is O(n). The hold and cash arrays use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Backward Decision DP
solutions.description:
## Approach
Work from the end of the price list toward the start. `free[day]` is the best future profit when you are free to buy, and `holding[day]` is the best future profit when you already hold a share. Buying moves from `free` to `holding`; selling moves from `holding` to `free[day + 2]`.

## Key Insight
The cooldown can be modeled as a jump over one day after selling. This suffix DP is the bottom-up version of the buy/sell recursion and makes the `day + 2` cooldown transition explicit without recursion.

## Complexity Analysis
Each day computes two suffix states, so the time complexity is O(n). The two arrays have length `n + 2` to make cooldown jumps safe, so the space complexity is O(n).

tests.description: Canonical cooldown example where selling forces a one-day wait before the next buy.
Single day cannot complete a transaction.
Two increasing prices allow one buy-sell profit.
Two decreasing prices should make no trade.
Monotone increasing prices are best handled by one long hold.
Monotone decreasing prices produce zero profit.
Flat prices produce no profitable transaction.
Long mixed sequence stresses cooldown state transitions across several decisions.
Best plan sells early, cools down, then buys the low price after the cooldown.
Small alternating prices catch solutions that rebuy immediately after selling.
Two profitable windows are separated by a cooldown-aware waiting period.
Skipping the early small sale enables buying the later zero and selling at four.
Multiple valleys and peaks require choosing sales that do not block later buys.
